recent_works.title: Inferring Titan Atmosphere Methane Content From Dragonfly Backshell Radiation Measurements
recent_works.abstract: During the entry of the Dragonfly capsule into the atmosphere of Titan, a variety of instruments will record vehicle surface properties including radiation. Uncertainty in CN emission remains a principal limitation in modeling and interpreting radiative heating during Titan atmospheric entry. Prior work has shown that the ratio of integrated CN red and CN violet band radiances can, in principle, be used to infer the freestream methane mole fraction when only chemical kinetic uncertainty is considered. In this study, we extend that framework to include uncertainty in the heavy-particle excitation rates governing the CN(A–X) and CN(B–X) band systems. The rates of these excitation processes are difficult to measure experimentally and exhibit discrepancies of multiple orders of magnitude across available datasets. Using polynomial chaos expansion surrogate models coupled with Bayesian inference in PyMC, we examine how methane identifiability evolves as excitation-rate uncertainty bounds are systematically tightened. recent_works.title: Integration of local and global surrogates for failure probability estimation
recent_works.abstract: This paper presents the development of an algorithm, termed the Global-Local Hybrid Surrogate (GLHS), designed to efficiently compute the probability of rare failure events in complex systems. The primary goal is to enhance the accuracy of reliability analysis while minimizing computational cost, particularly for high-dimensional problems where traditional methods, such as Monte Carlo simulations, become prohibitively expensive. The proposed GLHS builds upon the foundational work of Li et al., by integrating an adaptive strategy based on the General Domain Adaptive Strategy (Adcock et al.). The algorithm aims to approximate the failure domain of a given system, defined as the region in the input domain where the system transitions from safe to failure modes, described by a limit state surface. This failure domain is not explicitly known and must be learned iteratively during the analysis. The method employs a buffer zone, defined as the region surrounding the limit state surface.
